Parcel planning guide · reviewed 22 September 2026

LoloBuy volumetric weight: how to plan a smaller, safer parcel

A parcel is not priced by the product scale reading alone. Learn which measurements matter, where packaging changes the result, and what to check before treating any shipping figure as final.

Editorial note: This independent guide is based on LoloBuy’s public parcel, weight and packaging materials, checked on 22 September 2026. Route availability, billing rules and service options can change; confirm them in the live parcel screen before paying.

Why the warehouse weight is not the whole answer

A warehouse item can show a weight and still leave you with a poor international-shipping estimate. The recorded figure may include the item’s current packaging, while the final parcel will also have an outer carton or mailer, filler, tape and any reinforcement you request. If several items are consolidated, their shapes determine the final box. A light but bulky product can also be charged by the space it occupies rather than by its scale weight.

LoloBuy’s current public workflow separates the estimate from the finished parcel. It says the international shipping deposit is calculated from estimated weight, the chosen shipping method and the destination. It then says the final shipping fee is based on package size and weight verified by the shipping company. That distinction is the foundation of sensible planning: a warehouse number is useful input, not a guaranteed invoice.

The practical question is therefore not “How many kilograms are in My Warehouse?” It is “What package will these items create, and which weight will this route use for billing?” Answer that before route comparison and you will avoid many false bargains.

Actual weight, estimated weight and volumetric weight

Actual weight is the finished parcel on a scale

Actual weight is the physical weight after the selected items have been packed for dispatch. LoloBuy’s public weight guide describes a second weighing after a delivery order is submitted and the items and parcel packaging have been combined. That figure can differ from the earlier warehouse record because original packaging may be removed and shipping packaging may be added.

Do not subtract every shoe box or seller carton on paper and call the result “actual.” Some protective material may be retained, and the finished parcel still needs safe outer packaging. Actual weight exists only after the final packing decision has been carried out.

Estimated weight is a checkout-stage calculation

The same official guide describes estimated weight as the basis used when a shipment order is submitted. It combines warehouse-recorded weight with an allowance for the carton expected to hold the order. This lets the system request a deposit before the final parcel exists, but it is inherently provisional.

A change such as packaging removal can make the finished parcel lighter than the estimate. Conversely, protective packing or an awkward carton can move the result in the other direction. Treat the estimate as a budget checkpoint. Keep enough margin for a later adjustment and read the current account notice about how any difference is settled.

Volumetric weight converts space into a billing weight

Volumetric weight, sometimes called dimensional weight, uses the outside length, width and height of a parcel. The common structure is:

length × width × height ÷ route divisor

LoloBuy’s public help material currently lists a divisor of 6,000 for some preferential, dedicated and SF routes, and 5,000 for DHL, with dimensions measured in centimetres. A 50 × 40 × 30 cm parcel would therefore produce 10 kg with a 6,000 divisor and 12 kg with a 5,000 divisor. This is an illustration of why the selected route matters, not a promise that either route is available for your destination or item.

The same help page says international freight uses the greater of actual and volumetric weight as the billing weight. It also notes that some routes that generally do not calculate volumetric weight may still do so for unusually large items. Always use the divisor and exception rules shown for the live route rather than copying a formula from an old quote or another buyer’s parcel.

Find the item that is making the parcel expensive

Before submitting a parcel, classify each stored item by both mass and shape. Dense clothing, books and compact accessories usually add actual weight. Puffer jackets, plush items, hats, shoe boxes and product presentation boxes can add a disproportionate amount of volume. Fragile goods may need empty space and protection even if the item itself is small.

Write down the warehouse weight and external dimensions shown for every item. LoloBuy’s warehouse guidance says stored products are measured after packaging, including external length, width, height and weight. Those figures help you spot the likely problem item, but they do not predict the exact geometry after consolidation.

Then test the parcel concept, not just the sum. Ask whether one rigid box prevents soft goods from compressing, whether a long item forces a larger carton, or whether two fragile products need separation. Removing a 200-gram package can have little value if the parcel stays in the same billing increment. Shrinking one dimension enough to cross a volumetric threshold can matter more than removing additional grams.

Choose packaging by consequence, not by habit

Package removal can reduce weight and volume

LoloBuy’s current package-removal description says the free service can remove excess outer packaging when a delivery order is submitted. It presents choices ranging from removing only the shipping box to removing product boxes and bags. It also says necessary protective packaging—for example supports for vulnerable items or protective airbags—may be retained according to the actual situation.

That makes package removal a selective tool. It is a good candidate for disposable shoe boxes, retail sleeves or redundant seller cartons when presentation and resale condition do not matter. It is a poor default for collectibles, gift packaging, fragile goods or anything whose original box provides structural support. Once packaging is discarded, assume it cannot be restored.

Simple packing is not suitable for every item

The public simple-packing description says it is intended for non-fragile products and prioritizes a lightweight bag or stretch-film format, while allowing the warehouse to choose a carton when the goods require it. Soft clothing may suit this approach. Structured shoes, electronics, glass, ceramics or items with crush-sensitive surfaces may not.

Do not combine “remove everything” with “protect everything” in the same request. State the outcome you care about. For example: remove an undamaged retail shoe box only if it is not needed for protection, retain supports around a fragile component, or use simple packing only for the soft garments in the parcel. The warehouse still has to apply its handling standards.

Reinforcement can be worth the added weight

Reinforcement, corner protection or extra filler can increase actual weight and sometimes parcel dimensions. That is not automatically wasted cost. A compact but under-protected parcel is a poor optimization if normal handling can deform its contents. Use the lightest packaging that is appropriate for the item, not simply the lightest option listed.

Build three parcel scenarios before paying

A useful parcel plan compares three versions. The protective scenario keeps presentation boxes and adds suitable reinforcement. The balanced scenario removes redundant seller packaging but keeps structural protection. The compact scenario uses package removal and simple packing only for goods that can safely tolerate it.

For each scenario, note the likely actual-weight change, the likely dimension change and the risk you accept. Do not invent precise final dimensions. Instead, identify the condition that would make the choice worthwhile: “removing this box must shorten the parcel,” or “simple packing is useful only if all selected goods are non-fragile.” This turns a vague request to “make it cheaper” into a decision the warehouse can interpret.

Next, check the live route list for your destination and item types. A battery, liquid, magnetic part, branded product or unusually long item can change which routes appear. Route eligibility belongs after the item set and packaging plan are defined, because comparing a route that cannot carry the finished parcel is wasted work.

A pre-submission LoloBuy parcel checklist

Use this sequence before you authorize international dispatch:

  1. Confirm that every item has passed your warehouse QC decision.
  2. Record each item’s displayed weight and packaged dimensions.
  3. Identify the item most likely to drive length, width, height or protective space.
  4. Decide which retail or seller packaging may be removed and which protection must stay.
  5. Choose simple packing only for suitable non-fragile contents.
  6. Allow for the outer parcel and any reinforcement.
  7. Check the current route’s volumetric divisor, billing increment, restrictions and maximum dimensions.
  8. Compare actual and volumetric estimates; plan around the higher figure.
  9. Treat the payment-stage amount as a deposit until the packed parcel is verified.
  10. Save the packing request and review the final parcel details for unexpected changes.

If the difference between two scenarios is small, choose protection over a fragile saving. If a bulky, low-value item dominates the parcel, consider holding it for a different parcel rather than forcing an inefficient combination. Consolidation can reduce duplicate outer packaging, but it does not guarantee that every combination is cheaper.

Conclusion: optimize the box, not just the kilograms

The useful way to think about LoloBuy volumetric weight is to plan the finished package. Start with warehouse measurements, separate estimated weight from actual weight, apply the live route’s dimensional rule, and decide which packaging is genuinely redundant. A good parcel is neither the heaviest-protected nor the lightest-possible version. It is compact enough for the chosen route while preserving the protection the contents actually need.
